extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and compositors preparing copy for scholarly/publication (University of Chicago Press and similar academic publishers)
extracted.subtask_description: A University of Chicago Press style manual covering rules for capitalization, italics, quotations, spelling, and punctuation for preparing manuscripts and published material.

rubrics_metrics.name: 47. Capitalization of names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: The names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes (e.g., Kafir, Negro, Hottentot, Makassar, Buginese, Celestials) are treated as proper names for capitalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording and examples given: Kafir, Negro, Hottentot, Makassar, Buginese, Celestials.

rubrics_metrics.name: 48. Capitalization in astronomical work
rubrics_metrics.description: In astronomical work, capitalize the names of the bodies of our solar system except 'sun,' 'earth,' 'moon,' 'stars'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Milky Way, the Great Bear, Saturn.

rubrics_metrics.name: 49. Capitalization of university divisions, departments, officers, and courses in official work
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of divisions, departments, officers, and courses of study in official work dealing with administration or curricula (e.g., the University, the School of Education, the Department of Anthropology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lower-case forms in non-official references (but: the division, the department, the faculty). Examples: the Board of Trustees (the Trustees, the Board); Professor of Physics, Assistant in Chemistry, Fellow, Scholar; Van Husen Scholarship (but: the scholarship); courses in Political Economy, Autumn Quarter (but: a quarter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Capitals and Small Capitals for date line, salutatory, signature and residence
rubrics_metrics.description: Set the names of town and state in the date line, the salutatory phrase at the beginning of letters, and the signature and residence at the end of letters or articles in capitals and small capitals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format examples: 'Chicago, Ill., January 1, 1911' (set to the right, with one em's indention, preferably in smaller type than the body); 'My dear Mr. Smith:' (set flush, followed by a colon). Date and address layout guidance (centering, type size) also provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: 51. Use of 'Whereas', 'Note.', and 'Section' in formal documents
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions use 'Whereas'; in notes (not footnotes) use 'Note.' followed by a period and a dash; in constitutions and by-laws use 'Section' introducing paragraphs and followed by a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Note. — It should be noticed that ....' ; 'Section 1. This association shall be styled ....' Usual practice is to abbreviate 'Section' after the first occurrence (Sec 2.).

rubrics_metrics.name: 52. Set A.M., P.M., B.C., and A.D. in small capitals
rubrics_metrics.description: Set A.M., P.M., B.C., and A.D. in small capitals and without a space between letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '11:30 A.M.'; '53 B.C., 1906 A.D.' (see related cross-references).

rubrics_metrics.name: 53. Use small initial letters for formerly proper names now common
rubrics_metrics.description: Words of common usage originally proper names and their derivatives, and generally verbs derived from proper names, use small (lower-case) initial letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Utopia, bohemian, philistine, titanic, platonic, quixotic, bonanza, china, morocco, guinea-pig, boycott, roman (type), italicize, christianize, anglicize, macadamize.

rubrics_metrics.name: 54. Use small letters and abbreviations for minor literary subdivisions
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references use lower-case for minor subdivisions and their abbreviations (chapter, section, page, article, verse, line, note; chap., sec., p., art., vs., l., n.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See cross-references to related rules (37, 110, 237).

rubrics_metrics.name: 55. Abbreviations for units of measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Units of measurement should be abbreviated with lower-case initials (h.=hour, min.=minute, sec.=second; lb.=pound, oz.=ounce; yd.=yard, ft.=foot, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed: h., min., sec.; lb., oz.; yd., ft.; etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 56. Capitalization in italic side-heads
rubrics_metrics.description: In italic side-heads, capitalize only the first word and proper names; set all other words in lower-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules 172 and 280 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 57. Capitalization of first word of a quotation run into preceding text
rubrics_metrics.description: When a quotation is immediately connected with what precedes (e.g., through a conjunction), the first word of the quotation is treated as connected, even if in the original it begins a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See illustrations and exceptions in rules 35 and 131.

rubrics_metrics.name: 58. Use of italics for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words or phrases to which it is desired to lend emphasis or importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This was, however, not the case'; 'It is sufficiently plain that the sciences of life, at least, are studies of processes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 59. Italicize foreign-language words and short foreign passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words and phrases from foreign languages inserted into the English text and not incorporated into English; also single sentences or brief passages not long enough to call for reduced type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Darwinian Weltanschauung', 'Napoleon's coup d'état', 'de gustibus non est disputandum'. Do not italicize foreign titles preceding names or names of foreign institutions or anglicized words that have become part of English (examples: Père Lagrange, German Reichstag, Museo delle Terme; everyday anglicized words such as 'facade', 'resume').

rubrics_metrics.name: List of foreign/loanwords guidance (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provides a long illustrative list of foreign-origin words and their preferred typographic treatment under the italic rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive examples provided (a posteriori, ennui, percent, entree, apropos, ex cathedra, personnel, aide de camp, postmortem, etc.). Also notes when some of these are printed roman because anglicized.

rubrics_metrics.name: 60. Italicize titles of publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of publications—books, plays, essays, cycles of poems, pamphlets, treatises, tracts, documents, and periodicals—should be set in italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Spencer, Principles of Sociology; A Midsummer Night's Dream; the Chicago Tribune. Note: Books of the Bible and ancient manuscripts should be set in roman; exceptions for long bibliographies or tables where excessive italics is undesirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: 61. Italicize certain literary and legal reference words
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words and abbreviations used in literary and legal references such as ad hoc, circa (ca.), et al., ibid., idem, infra, loc. cit., op. cit., passim, sic, supra, s.v., vide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not italicize cf., e.g., i.e., v. (versus), viz., etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 62. Italicize 'See' and 'See also' in indexes and 'for'/'read' in errata lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Set 'See' and 'See also' in italics in an index or similar compilation to differentiate; in errata lists set 'for' and 'read' in italics to separate them from incorrect and correct readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'See also Sociology'; 'for levee read levée.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 63. Italicize plaintiff and defendant names in legal citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize the names of plaintiff and defendant in legal citations, and titles of proceedings containing prefixes like in re, ex parte, In the matter of, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Conolly v. Union Sewer Pipe Co.; In re Smith; Ex parte Brown; In the matter of the petition of Henry Robinson for a writ of habeas corpus.

rubrics_metrics.name: 64. Format and capitalization of address lines in speeches and letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Address lines in speeches, reports, and primary address lines in letters should be set flush as a separate line, with nouns capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen:'; 'Mr. John Smith, 321 Dearborn Street, Chicago, Ill.'; 'Dear Sir: I take pleasure...' (see 50 for related rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: 65. Formatting of signatures and appended titles
rubrics_metrics.description: In signatures, the position or title after the name is run into the same line if one word; if more than one word but not longer than the name, center the first letter under the name and indent one em on the right; if longer than the name, center the name over the second line and set the title flush.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Examples: 'Arthur P. Maguire, Secretary' ; 'Carter H. Harrison
Mayor of Chicago' ; 'Charles M. Gayley
Professor of English Language and Literature'. Rules subject to exigencies of special cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: 66. Use of a), b), c) and a, b, c letter affixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a), b), c), etc. to indicate subdivisions (single parenthesis if beginning a paragraph, double parentheses if run in); use a, b, c, etc. affixed to numbers of verse/page to denote fractional part (e.g., Luke 4:31a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting distinction between paragraph-beginning vs run-in usage provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: 67. Use of letters to designate unknown quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters are used to designate unknown quantities, lines, etc., in algebraic, geometrical, and similar matter (e.g., ac+bc=...; lines a and b; the nth power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ac+bc=..., the lines a and b, the nth power.

rubrics_metrics.name: 68. Use of letters referencing illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters used in legends or in the text that refer to corresponding letters in accompanying illustrations should be set as letters (e.g., 'At the point A above (see diagram)').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule applies as a general practice for legends and references to diagrams.

rubrics_metrics.name: 69. References to particular letters
rubrics_metrics.description: When referring to particular letters, set them as references (example fragment given: the letter u, a small v).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in text show typographic treatment for references to letters themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: 70. Shillings and pence abbreviations after numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 's.' and 'd.' (= shillings and pence) following numerals (e.g., 35s. 6d.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 270 for further context.

rubrics_metrics.name: 71. Italicize scientific (Latin) names of genera and species
rubrics_metrics.description: In zoological, geological, and paleontological matter, scientific (Latin) names of genera and species when used together should be italicized, with the generic name in nominative singular. In botanical/geological/paleontological matter italicize genera and species when used together, and genera alone when used alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Felis leo, Rosa Carolina, Canodectes favosus, Phyteuma Ederi. Note: In medical matter the general practice is to print such names in roman (avoid italics).

rubrics_metrics.name: 71a. Astronomical naming and italics exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: In astronomical and astrophysical matter: (a) italicize Greek, Latin, and Arabic names of planets, satellites, constellations, and individual stars; (b) italicize designations of celestial objects in well-known catalogs and Flamsteed/Bayer designations; (c) chemical element symbols are not italicized; (d) lower-case letters designating certain Fraunhofer lines are italicized but capital Fraunhofer letters and spectral type letters are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jupiter, Tethys, Lyra, Antares; M1, N.G.C. 6165; H, Ca, Ti (chemical symbols not italicized); Fraunhofer lower-case letters a, b, g, A (italicized) but A-H and K (not italicized); spectral types As, B3, M8 (not italicized).

rubrics_metrics.name: 72. Capitalize 'Resolved.' in resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions the word 'Resolved.' should be used (capitalized) to introduce resolved clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 39 for related practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 73. Use 'Continued' after headlines and 'To be continued' at ends
rubrics_metrics.description: After headlines or titles, as a rule, use the word 'Continued' and use 'To be continued' at the end of articles when continuation is intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'THE SCOPE OF SOCIOLOGY—Continued' and notation '[To be continued]'. See rule 179 for continuation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 74. Use quotation marks for run-in citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Put between quotation marks (and in roman type) citations run into the text of a passage from an author in his own words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 85 for rules about reduced type for longer extracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: 75. Quotations from different authors/works adjacent should be marked
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations from different authors, or from different works by the same author, following each other uninterrupted by intervening original matter (or other than a footnote reference) should be set in quotation marks even if reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules 85–87 for reduced citation exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 76. Use quotes for a word or phrase accompanied by its definition
rubrics_metrics.description: When a word or phrase is accompanied by its definition, enclose the term in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '"Drop-folio" means a page-number at the foot of the page.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 77. Use quotes for unusual, technical, ironical, or highlighted words/phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Place in quotation marks an unusual, technical, ironical, etc., word or phrase in the text (whether or not accompanied by a directional word like 'so-called').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Her 'five o'clocks' were famous; He was elected 'master of the rolls'; This so-called 'man of affairs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 78. Use quotes for English equivalents in translations
rubrics_metrics.description: In translations, enclose the English equivalent of a foreign word, phrase, or passage in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Weltanschauung, 'world-view' or 'fundamental aspect of life'; Mommsen Romische Geschichte ('History of Rome').

rubrics_metrics.name: 79. Use quotes to direct attention to particular words or terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Put in quotation marks the particular word or words to which attention is directed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the term 'lynch law'; the phrase 'liberty of conscience'; the concepts 'good' and 'bad'; the name 'Chicago.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 80. Serial titles in quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Set serial titles (series titles) in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'English Men of Letters' series; 'International Critical Commentary.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 81. Titles of shorter poems in quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of shorter poems should be put in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Shelley's 'To a Skylark.' (See 60 for longer works.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 82. Use quotes for titles of subdivisions, papers, lectures, etc.; special handling for Preface/Introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Cited titles of subdivisions (parts, books, chapters), titles of papers, lectures, sermons, toasts, mottoes, etc., should be in quotation marks; references to Preface, Introduction, Table of Contents, Index, etc., of a specific work should be set with capitals and without quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Beginnings of the Science of Political Economy, Vol. I, 'The British School,' chap. ii, 'John Stuart Mill'; Preface, p. iii (no quotes). Note: Botanical Gazette footnote practice differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: 83. Names of ships in quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of ships should be placed in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the U.S. SS. 'Oregon'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 84. Titles of pictures and works of art in quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the titles of pictures and works of art in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Murillo's 'The Holy Family.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 85. Set long prose and poetry extracts in smaller type
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily set in smaller type all prose extracts that will make five or more lines in the smaller type, and all poetry citations of two lines or more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An isolated prose quotation may be run into the text if it bears organic relation to the argument; a short quotation near longer reduced extracts may be reduced for uniform appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 86. Reduction of point size for reduced citations
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, reduce from 11-pt and 10-pt to 9-pt, from 9-pt to 8-pt, from 8-pt to 6-pt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 252 for further typographic sizing guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 87. Reduced citations omit quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduced citations should not have quotation marks, except in cases noted in rule 75; as a rule, quotation marks should not be used in connection with italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions and special cases referenced (see 75).

rubrics_metrics.name: 88. Quotation marks should include ellipses and 'etc.' when part of quoted matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks should include ellipses and the phrase 'etc.' when they are part of the quoted matter; perfect clearness in each case is the best criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative examples explain when 'etc.' belongs inside vs outside the quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: 89. Repeat opening quotation marks for multi-paragraph quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted prose broken into paragraphs should have the opening quotation marks repeated at the beginning of each paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures clarity that the quoted material continues across paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: 90. 'Clearing' quotation marks for alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Where alignment is desired, quotation marks should be 'cleared'—i.e., project beyond the line of alignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example demonstrates opening quotation mark projecting beyond left margin for alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: 91. Use double quotes for primary quotations and alternate with single quotes for nested quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Double quotation marks are used for primary quotations; a quotation within a quotation uses single marks; alternate back to double for a third level, single for a fourth, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative nested-quotation example provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: 92. Spell out civil and military titles preceding names (exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out all civil and military titles and forms of address when they precede the name, except Mr., Messrs., Mrs., Dr., Rev., Hon.; omit 'Rev.' and 'Hon.' except in quotations; abbreviate Esq. when following the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Macmillan & Co., Mr. Smith; uses of French abbreviations also noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: 93. Spell out Christian names and 'von' as part of name
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out Christian names (George, Charles, John) rather than using abbreviations (Geo., Chas., Jno.), except where the abbreviated form is used in quoted matter or original signatures; retain 'von' as part of a person's name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 240 for additional guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 94. Spell out numbers under three digits in ordinary reading-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter, spell out all numbers of less than three digits unless of a statistical or technical character, or unless occurring in long groups; treat connected groups alike—if the largest contains three or more digits use figures for all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and exceptions: 'There are thirty-eight cities...' but 'He spent 128 days...' Use figures for decimals, degrees, dimensions, distances, enumerations, money, percentages, weights, etc. (10^, 45 miles, 3 cubic feet, 24 pages, 100 bushels, 9 per cent, $1,000).

rubrics_metrics.name: 95. Spell out round approximate numbers; use figures for more precise
rubrics_metrics.description: Round numbers (approximate) are usually spelled out (e.g., 'five hundred'), but approximate figures that are more precise (e.g., 550) use figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The attendance was estimated at five hundred' (but use 'at 550' if more precise). Use 'fifteen hundred' rather than 'one thousand five hundred' if 1500 is spelled out.

rubrics_metrics.name: 96. Spell out numbers that begin sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: All numbers, no matter how high, commencing a sentence in ordinary reading-matter should be spelled out; when impracticable, reconstruct the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Five hundred and ninety-three men, 417 women...' When impractical, rewrite: 'The total number ... was 593 men.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 97. Spell out sums of money in isolated cases; use figures when many
rubrics_metrics.description: Sums of money occurring in isolated cases in ordinary reading-matter should be spelled out ('The admission was two dollars'); when several monetary figures occur close together or in statistical material, use figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Admission: men, $2; women, $1; children, 25 cents.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 98. Time of day spell-out vs figures depending on context
rubrics_metrics.description: Time of day in ordinary reading-matter is spelled out ('at four; at half-past two in the afternoon'); in statistical/enumerative contexts and with A.M./P.M. use figures (at 4:15 P.M.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit 'o'clock' in statistical forms with figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: 99. Ages should be spelled out
rubrics_metrics.description: Ages in ordinary reading-matter should be spelled out (eighty years and four months old; children between six and fourteen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use words for ages in narrative contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: 100. Spell out numbers of centuries, dynasties, sessions etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers of centuries, Egyptian dynasties, sessions of Congress, military bodies, political divisions, thoroughfares, and similar cases should be spelled out unless brevity is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nineteenth century; Fifth Dynasty; Fifty-fourth Congress, Second Session; Fifteenth Infantry N.G.; Sixth Congressional District, Second Ward; Fifth Avenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: 101. Use phrases for decades
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to particular decades in phrases such as 'in the nineties.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short decade references spelled out as words.

rubrics_metrics.name: 102. Spell out names of months except in statistical or long enumerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the full name of months (January, February, etc.) except in statistical matter or long enumerations where figures/abbreviations may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'from January 1 to April 15' (omit st, nd, th after dates).

rubrics_metrics.name: 103. Use 'United States' spelled out with exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'United States' spelled out except in quotations and certain connections (e.g., General Schofield, U.S.A.; U.S. SS. 'Oregon'); in footnotes and similar references abbreviate as U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference rules 22, 52, 106 for other abbreviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 104. Use full forms for Railroad, Fort, Mount, and Port in place names
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out Railroad (not R.R. or Ry.) and use full forms for Fort, Mount, and Port in geographical appellations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad; Fort Wayne; Port Huron; Mount Elias.

rubrics_metrics.name: 105. Spell out names of publications in most cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases, spell out names of publications; rule open to modification in particular instances—expediency, context, authoritative usage, and author's preference may justify exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If in doubt, spell out; good taste condones spelling out more readily than abbreviation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 106. Abbreviate state names following town names per specified list
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of states, territories, and possessions of the United States following towns should be abbreviated according to a specified list and without a space between abbreviation letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a table of state abbreviations (Ala., Ariz., Cal., etc.) and special cases (D.C., P.I. for Philippine Islands, P.R. = Porto Rico, etc.). See cross-references (22, 52, 103).

rubrics_metrics.name: 107. Abbreviate Company, Brothers, and use ampersand in technical bibliographic matter
rubrics_metrics.description: In technical matter (footnotes, bibliographies), abbreviate 'Company' and 'Brothers', and use the ampersand (&) in firm names; in narrative text these words may be spelled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Macmillan Co., Macmillan & Co., Harper Bros.; in text 'Harper Brothers have recently published ...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 108. Abbreviate 'Saint' as 'St.' in place names with exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'St.' for 'Saint' before place names and churches (St. Louis, St. Peter's Church), but preferably omit 'St.' before names of apostles, evangelists, and church fathers (Luke, Paul, Augustine—not St. Luke, St. Paul, St. Augustine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to ecclesiastical naming conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 109. Abbreviations for books of the Bible and Apocrypha
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide standard abbreviations for books of the Old and New Testaments and Apocrypha (Gen., Exod., Lev., Ps., Matt., Mark, Luke, John, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also lists common versions abbreviations (A.V., R.V., A.R.V., E.V., Vulg., LXX).

rubrics_metrics.name: 110. Abbreviate bibliographical terms (Vol., No., p., pp., etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references, footnotes, and bibliographical material abbreviate 'volume', 'number', 'psalm', 'division', 'chapter', 'article', 'section', 'page', 'column', 'verse', 'line', 'note', 'figure' followed by their number (Vol., No., Ps., Div., chap., art., sec., p., col., vs., l., n., Fig.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides forms for pluralization and for indicating 'following' pages (pp. 5 f.; pp. 5 ff.).

rubrics_metrics.name: 111. Use metric and common measurement abbreviations after numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use common metric and measurement symbols when following a numeral (1 m., 2 dm., 3 cm., 4 mm.; cm. = cubic meter, gm. = gram, lb. = pound, oz. = ounce, yd., ft., in.; A.U. = Angstrom units, H.P. = horse-power, C. = Centigrade, F. = Fahrenheit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists common symbols and cross-references other rules (see 123).

rubrics_metrics.name: 112. Handling extracts from modern vs Old English authors
rubrics_metrics.description: In extracts from modern authors whose spelling and punctuation differ slightly from modern usage, use office style; in citations from Old English works or where fidelity is essential, follow the original copy. Titles should always be accurately quoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose fidelity to original only when necessary for writer's plan or context.

rubrics_metrics.name: 113. Forming possessives of proper names ending in s or sibilant
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the possessive of proper names ending in s or another sibilant: if the name is monosyllabic, add apostrophe + s (King James's Version); if more than one syllable, add apostrophe alone (Moses').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: King James's Version, Burns's poems, Moses' law, Demosthenes' orations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 114. Use 'a' before sounded h, long w, and 'one'
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sounded h, long w, and the word 'one' use the indefinite article 'a' rather than 'an' (a hotel, a harmonic, a historical, a union, such a one).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance pertains to euphony and pronunciation-based article choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 115. Use and avoid ligatures in Latin and other languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use the ligatures æ and œ (separate the letters) in quotations from Latin and anglicized derivatives from Latin or Greek through Latin where e has not been substituted; retain the ligature in quotations from Old English and from French and other modern languages when following another vowel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Aurea prima sata est...' and anglicized words like 'the Aeneid', 'Oedipus Tyrannus', 'Caesar', 'aesthetic', 'subpoena' (separated). Retain ligatures in French titles where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: 116. Distinguish 'farther' and 'further'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'farther' for physical distance ('more remote', 'at a greater distance') and 'further' in the sense of 'moreover' or 'in addition'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the farther end'; 'further, he suggested'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 117. Use 'O' without comma in vocative; 'Oh,' with comma for exclamation
rubrics_metrics.description: In forms of address (vocative) use 'O' without a following comma; for an exclamation use 'Oh,' followed by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'O thou most mighty ruler!' vs 'Oh, why did not Cerberus drag me back to hell?'

rubrics_metrics.name: 118. Participles retaining final 'e' and those that omit
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain participles retain the final 'e' (agreeing, hieing, singeing, dyeing, hoeing, tingeing, eyeing, shoeing, vieing); others omit the 'e' before the terminal (acknowledging, gluing, judging, awing, grudging, owing, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists examples distinguishing retention vs omission of final 'e'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 119. Preferred American spellings and closed compounds guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Provides a long list of preferred spellings (American forms) and guidance to make one word of compounds like 'anyone', 'someone', 'everyone', 'today', 'tomorrow', 'tonight', 'cannot', and to distinguish 'sometimes' vs 'some time(s)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive authoritative list given (abridgment, center, favor, honor, color, theater, program, etc.). Note: In official University of Chicago publications 'comptroller' preferred in that one case.

rubrics_metrics.name: 120. Distinguish -ise and -ize verb endings per list
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate which verbs take -ise vs -ize endings, with two columns listing verbs that should be spelled with -ise (advertise, comprise, advise, etc.) and with -ize (aggrandize, analyze, baptize, apologize, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensive lists are provided indicating the preferred termination for many verbs (see the two-column lists).

rubrics_metrics.name: 121. Punctuation marks printed in same style/font as preceding word
rubrics_metrics.description: All punctuation marks should be printed in the same style or font of type as the word or letter immediately preceding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'With the cry of Banzai!' ; 'Luke 4:16a/ No. 1.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 122. Period marks the end of a complete sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: A period is used to indicate the end of a complete sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See related rule 125 for exceptions where periods are omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: 123. Use period after abbreviations with exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a period after all abbreviations except in cases where mechanical necessity compels omission (e.g., certain metric/format notations); treat metric symbols as abbreviations (with periods) but not chemical symbols, nor 'per cent', nor book formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Macmillan & Co., Mr. Smith, No. 1, Chas. ; but chemical symbols O, Fe; 2 per cent; typographic exceptions (Astrophysical Journal uses '12 mm' with no period). Also exceptions for recognized abbreviations of linguistic epochs and initials of well-known publications (AJSL, ZAW) where no periods are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: 124. No period after Roman numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use no period after Roman numerals, even when they have the value of ordinals (Vol. IV; Louis XVI was on the throne).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roman numerals remain without trailing period.

rubrics_metrics.name: 125. Omit periods after running-heads, certain headings, date lines, and signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the period after running-heads, centered headlines, side-heads set in separate lines, cut-in heads, box-heads in tables, and superscriptions/legends which do not form a complete sentence; also omit after date lines and signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 50 for related signature/date guidance; relates to headline and running-head formatting (see 279–283 for definitions).

rubrics_metrics.name: 126. Period placement with quotation marks and parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the period inside the quotation marks; place a period inside parentheses only when the parenthetical matter is an independent sentence; otherwise place it outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as 'a rule without exception' for periods inside quotation marks. Examples provided for both cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: 127. Use of exclamation point
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the exclamation point to mark an outcry, or an emphatic or ironical utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Long live the king!' 'Heaven forbid!' 'How funny this seems!'

rubrics_metrics.name: 128. Exclamation point placement with quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclamation point is placed inside the quotation marks when it is part of the quotation; otherwise it is placed outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See examples under rule 127.

rubrics_metrics.name: 129. Use of interrogation (question) point
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the interrogation point to mark a query or to express doubt; do not use an interrogation point after indirect questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Who is this?' but 'He asked whether he was ill.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 130. Question mark placement with quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the interrogation point inside the quotation marks only when the question is part of the quotation; otherwise place it outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate quoted questions vs surrounding sentence questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 131. Use of the colon
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon marks a discontinuity of grammatical construction greater than a semicolon and less than a period; commonly used (1) to emphasize close connection between two complete clauses, (2) to separate a complete clause from an illustrative/amplifying clause, (3) to introduce a formal statement, extract, or speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (1) 'This argument undeniably contains some force: Thus it is well known that...'; (2) 'Most countries have a national flower: France the lily, England the rose'; (3) 'The rule may be stated thus: ...' Also guidance on using comma before mid-sentence quotations instead of colon.

rubrics_metrics.name: 132. Colon as substitute for 'namely/as follows' and punctuation after such phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon often takes the place of 'namely', 'as follows', 'for instance'; when such a word or phrase is used, it should be followed by a colon if what follows consists of one or more grammatically complete clauses, otherwise by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This is true of only two nations...: Great Britain and France' (colon used); contrasts given where a comma is appropriate when the following is not a complete clause.
